Ethanol acutely modulates inhibitory GABA-A signaling in neuronal preparations. This pharmacological effect is distinct from chronic receptor redistribution and does not imply identical effects at every receptor subtype.
Ethanol inhibits NMDA-receptor-mediated calcium influx in the reviewed neuronal experiments; the acute receptor action is separate from chronic glutamate adaptation.
Drinking produces an opioid-sensitive PET ligand-displacement response in human accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex; the intervening release machinery is not resolved by this experiment.
Alcohol engages mesolimbic reinforcement circuitry through several neuronal and receptor routes; the dopamine synthesis does not establish one exclusive upstream relay.
Single and repeated ethanol regimens alter receptor trafficking and surface composition in rodents. The exact signaling route and persistence depend on the regimen and neuronal compartment.
Exposure and withdrawal are associated with altered glutamate regulation. Human regional measurements and repeated-vapor rodent experiments do not imply a single uniform trajectory.
The withdrawal framework recruits extended-amygdala CRF systems after repeated drug exposure; complete mediation of the human stress response remains unresolved.
Dependent-animal and neurocircuitry evidence implicates dynorphin signaling in withdrawal-related stress, without establishing its recruitment as universal in AUD.
Withdrawal from chronic exposure lowers dopamine activity in reviewed rodent experiments; the transition to a human subjective reward deficit requires additional interpretation.
Repeated seeking and reinforcement permit habitual control to develop in the rat paradigm; the predictor relationship does not prove that exposure alone determines later compulsivity.
Heavy drinking can reduce nutritional intake and impair thiamine availability. These known nutritional intermediates are not expanded into separate nodes here.
Chronic ethanol exposure produces TLR4-dependent inflammatory responses in mouse and astrocyte models; the experiments do not establish ethanol as a direct TLR4 ligand.
Repeated pairing and learning offer an interpretation of cue-associated responses; the imaging synthesis alone does not prove longitudinal sensitization.
The framework describes an exposure-associated contribution to executive dysfunction; pre-existing liability and other factors cannot be excluded by cross-sectional imaging.
Withdrawal after sustained heavy exposure can activate autonomic responses in physiologically dependent individuals.
Alcohol metabolism and disturbed lipid handling connect sustained exposure to hepatic fat accumulation; those known liver-specific intermediates are curated in Alcoholic_Liver_Disease.
Repeated liver injury, inflammation and fibrotic remodeling connect chronic exposure to cirrhosis; those established intermediate processes are outside this AUD graph.
Chronic alcohol toxicity can produce myocardial injury and adverse remodeling before ventricular dilation; the organ-specific intermediates are not expanded here.
Alcohol-related pancreatic injury and inflammation can lead to acute or chronic pancreatitis through organ-specific pathways omitted from this graph.
Direct neurotoxicity and nutritional injury are recognized routes from chronic alcohol use to peripheral neuropathy; the nerve-specific intermediates are not expanded here.
Ethanol is converted by ADH enzymes to acetaldehyde; accumulation depends on the balance between this known formation step and ALDH-mediated clearance.
Faster formation may increase local or transient acetaldehyde exposure; systemic accumulation and symptom severity also depend on clearance.
Reduced aldehyde oxidation impairs acetaldehyde clearance during alcohol exposure.
Acetaldehyde accumulation elicits downstream vasoactive and autonomic responses that contribute to aversion; these physiological intermediates are not expanded in this graph.
Flushing is one component of the exposure-dependent aversive reaction.
Alcohol-evoked opioid signaling provides a reward-related input that may promote continued use; this PET experiment does not demonstrate the intervening steps to loss of control.
Dopamine-dependent reinforcement can strengthen alcohol-directed behavior, while the transition to impaired control involves additional learning and executive processes.
Cue-related circuit responses correlate with behavior, but the imaging synthesis does not prove that those responses cause later loss of control.
Brain cue responses can correlate with reported craving, but association does not establish a necessary causal circuit.

Changes in inhibitory or excitatory synaptic signaling alter neuronal excitability when ethanol is reduced. These known physiological intermediates are summarized here; their relative contribution differs across models and patients.

Withdrawal-related neural hyperexcitability can manifest as tremor through motor-system output.
Excessive synchronized neuronal activity can produce a generalized withdrawal seizure in susceptible patients.
Severe withdrawal can impair attention and awareness through distributed brain dysfunction; hyperexcitability is contributory rather than a complete explanation of delirium.
Withdrawal-associated circuit dysfunction can produce hallucinations; the precise sensory-network mediation is incompletely resolved.
Withdrawal-related arousal can disrupt sleep through central sleep-wake regulation.
Withdrawal can produce nausea and vomiting through central and autonomic responses; the cited clinical account does not resolve their exact mediation.
Sympathetic efferent signaling increases cardiac rate during withdrawal.
Autonomic sudomotor output increases sweating during withdrawal.
Autonomic cardiovascular output can raise blood pressure during withdrawal.

Relief of aversive withdrawal states can motivate renewed use through negative reinforcement; this does not account for all patterns of impaired control.
Anxiety can be part of an aversive withdrawal state, without implying all independent anxiety disorders arise through this route.
In the rat paradigm, stronger habitual control predicted punishment-resistant seeking; extrapolation to human impaired control remains indirect.
Reduced executive regulation can make limiting use more difficult, but imaging and review evidence do not establish one necessary causal pathway.
This clinical domain is represented in the review framework; severity and cause vary among individuals.
The node describes the impaired-control component of the clinical phenotype, while individual DSM criterion combinations vary.
Persistent impaired control can produce problematic consumption and related impairment.
Difficulty limiting use can perpetuate exposure, creating a feedback relationship rather than a necessary one-way progression.

TLR4 signals through intracellular adaptor and kinase pathways to NF-kappa-B. Astrocyte knockdown supports this route, while the intervening canonical signaling steps are not separate graph nodes.
Constitutive Tlr4 deletion prevents the measured cortical cytokine induction in this mouse regimen; cell-specific production and all intervening routes remain unresolved.
Tlr4 deletion attenuates cortical GFAP reactivity but leaves a residual response; the experiment does not isolate every intervening glial signal.
The mouse comparison associates TLR4 function with ethanol-induced cortical caspase-3 cleavage; the responsible cell type and intervening death pathway remain unresolved.
Regional pharmacological perturbation altered intake in nondependent DID mice; the intervening neuronal mechanism and human relevance are unresolved.
Repeated consumption supplies ethanol exposure.
Repeated exposure promotes longer-lasting receptor remodeling in reviewed rodent protocols; the intermediate steps and human time course are unresolved.

nodes.description: Reduced clearance, or an imbalance between formation and clearance, increases exposure to the toxic ethanol metabolite acetaldehyde. This conditional metabolic branch is especially well supported for reduced ALDH2 activity.

evidence.reference_title: The genetics of alcohol metabolism: role of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase variants.
evidence.snippet: A variant of the ALDH2 gene encodes an essentially inactive ALDH enzyme, resulting in acetaldehyde accumulation

nodes.description: Flushing, nausea and tachycardia after acetaldehyde accumulation can discourage drinking. This is a protective modifier pathway, not an obligatory step in the progression of AUD. Disulfiram deliberately engages an aversive response by inhibiting aldehyde clearance.

evidence.reference_title: The genetics of alcohol metabolism: role of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase variants.
evidence.snippet: Acetaldehyde is a toxic substance whose accumulation leads to a highly aversive reaction that includes facial flushing, nausea, and rapid heart beat (i.e., tachycardia).

nodes.description: Acute ethanol can enhance GABAergic inhibition through effects that depend on receptor composition, synaptic compartment, dose and brain region. The review evidence includes rodent and cellular work; it does not establish uniform potentiation at every receptor or a single necessary route to human intoxication. GABAergic neurons supply the inhibitory transmitter; receptor-bearing target neurons need not themselves be GABAergic.

evidence.reference_title: Targeting glutamate uptake to treat alcohol use disorders.
evidence.snippet: the acute actions of ethanol are to inhibit glutamatergic activity and potentiate GABAergic activity.

nodes.description: Experimental literature describes inhibition of NMDA-receptor-mediated calcium influx by ethanol. This acute receptor effect is distinct from chronic changes in receptor trafficking, glutamate release and uptake.

evidence.reference_title: Targeting glutamate uptake to treat alcohol use disorders.
evidence.snippet: Intracellularly, ethanol inhibits, non-competitively, the NMDAR-mediated calcium influx in the cortex, Acb, amygdala, hippocampus, and VTA (Nie et al., 1994; Wirkner et al., 2000; Roberto et al., 2004; Stobbs et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2007).

nodes.description: Impaired control, unsuccessful attempts to reduce use and continued use despite harm may characterize AUD. DSM-5-TR requires a combination of criteria, so no single control symptom or withdrawal finding is mandatory in every case.

evidence.reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of AUD can be made when a patient has a problematic pattern of alcohol use over a year that leads to clinically significant impairment or distress, involving at least 2 of the 11 DSM-5-TR criteria.

nodes.description: Alpha-2 agonists or beta-blockers may be added for persistent autonomic symptoms in selected patients. They do not prevent or treat withdrawal seizures or delirium and must not replace effective withdrawal therapy.

evidence.snippet: They should not be used alone to prevent or treat withdrawal-related seizures or delirium.

nodes.description: Alcohol-associated cues evoke brain responses that can correlate with craving. The meta-analysis included 28 studies of heavy-drinking/AUD samples; within-case ventral-striatal activation was not equivalent to a significant case-versus-control difference. Region-of-interest selection, heterogeneous ascertainment and mainly male samples limit generalization. This is an associative circuit finding, not a validated clinical biomarker.

evidence.reference_title: Functional neuroimaging studies of alcohol cue reactivity: a quantitative meta-analysis and systematic review.
evidence.snippet: Among cases, alcohol cues elicited robust activation of limbic and prefrontal regions, including ventral striatum, anterior cingulate and ventromedial prefrontal cortex.

evidence.reference_title: Functional neuroimaging studies of alcohol cue reactivity: a quantitative meta-analysis and systematic review.
evidence.snippet: Cue-elicited activation of ventral striatum was most frequently correlated with behavioral measures and most frequently reduced by treatment, but these results were often derived from region-of-interest analyses that interrogated only limbic regions.

nodes.description: Withdrawal delirium combines disturbed attention and awareness with confusion, often hallucinations and autonomic activation. It is a potentially life-threatening complication requiring close monitoring, and other causes of delirium must also be assessed.

evidence.reference_title: https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
evidence.snippet: If untreated or inadequately treated, withdrawal can progress to generalized tonic-clonic seizures, delirium tremens, and death.

nodes.description: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures can complicate alcohol withdrawal, typically during the first 12–48 hours after cessation or marked reduction. They can occur despite treatment, and assessment must consider other seizure causes.

evidence.reference_title: https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
evidence.snippet: If untreated or inadequately treated, withdrawal can progress to generalized tonic-clonic seizures, delirium tremens, and death.

nodes.description: Alcohol intake supplies the exposure required for alcohol-related reinforcement and complications. Repeated heavy exposure can produce receptor adaptations in experimental paradigms, but exposure does not inevitably lead to AUD. Effects depend on dose, timing and host context.

evidence.reference_title: Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
evidence.snippet: The fact that not every person who drinks alcohol will necessarily experience a loss of control and progression to addiction indicates that AUD is not solely driven by exposure to alcohol.

nodes.description: Human positron-emission tomography after drinking showed displacement of a mu-opioid radioligand in nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex, interpreted as endogenous opioid release. This is an indirect release measure; the study did not identify the peptide, resolve a dopamine relay, or test naltrexone efficacy.

evidence.reference_title: Alcohol consumption induces endogenous opioid release in the human orbitofrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens.
evidence.snippet: Drinking alcohol induced opioid release in the nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex, areas of the brain implicated in reward valuation.

nodes.description: Review of selected rats with voluntary ethanol intake, reinforcement and protocol-dependent binge/deprivation responses. The historical animal criteria are not DSM-5-TR criteria, and neither human age at onset nor all AUD domains are reproduced. Intoxicating concentrations depend on the access paradigm.

evidence.reference_title: The alcohol-preferring (P) and high-alcohol-drinking (HAD) rats--animal models of alcoholism.
evidence.snippet: The P line of rats meets all of the originally proposed criteria for a suitable animal model of alcoholism.

evidence.reference_title: The alcohol-preferring (P) and high-alcohol-drinking (HAD) rats--animal models of alcoholism.
evidence.snippet: The P line also exhibits excessive binge-like alcohol drinking, attaining blood alcohol concentrations (BACs) of 200 mg% on a daily basis.

nodes.description: Repeated ethanol exposure and withdrawal can alter glutamate release, uptake and receptor regulation. Elevated extracellular glutamate is supported in particular rodent dependence models, while human spectroscopy results vary by region and timing and do not all show elevation. The whole process should not be reduced to universal NMDA-receptor upregulation.

evidence.reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
evidence.snippet: Some studies have reported reduced cortical glutamate levels associated with dependence and acute withdrawal (Mon et al., 2012; Ende et al., 2013), while other studies have shown elevated glutamate activity in anterior cingulate and striatum in alcohol-dependent subjects (Hermann et al., 2012; Bauer et al., 2013).

evidence.reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
evidence.snippet: Repeated cycles of chronic intermittent exposure to alcohol vapor were shown to increase basal levels of glutamate in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) at time points beyond acute withdrawal.

nodes.description: Anxiety can accompany withdrawal or the negative-affect component of dependence; independent anxiety disorders may also coexist. Persistence and mechanisms vary among individuals.

nodes.description: First-line medication for moderate to severe alcohol withdrawal and prevention or treatment of withdrawal seizures and delirium, with monitoring for oversedation and respiratory depression. Symptom-triggered protocols require reliable assessment; fixed or front-loading approaches may be appropriate. Agent selection and dosing depend on liver function, comorbidity and setting. This is a short-course withdrawal treatment, not ongoing AUD pharmacotherapy.

nodes.description: The addiction framework implicates CRF signaling in dependence-related stress and negative affect, with much of the causal evidence from rodent regional pharmacology. evidence.reference_title: Neurobiology of addiction: a neurocircuitry analysis.
evidence.snippet: The increases in negative emotional states and dysphoric and stress-like responses in the withdrawal/negative affect stage involve decreases in the function of the dopamine component of the reward system and recruitment of brain stress neurotransmitters, such as corticotropin-releasing factor and dynorphin, in the neurocircuitry of the extended amygdala.

nodes.description: Starting at 7 weeks, mice received 10% ethanol in drinking water for 5 months; reported intake and blood alcohol concentrations were similar between genotypes. Neither alcohol seeking, cognition nor neuron-specific death was directly tested.

Effects depend on timing, region, sex and model; knockout findings are not uniform. Injectable-specific efficacy evidence is smaller and outcome-dependent; it should not be assumed superior to oral medication or to eliminate adherence problems. The same opioid-related precautions apply.

evidence.snippet: Naltrexone is a mu-opioid receptor antagonist that can be taken daily by mouth or as a monthly intramuscular injection administered in the clinic setting.

evidence.snippet: Fewer data were available for the 100-mg/d oral and injectable doses.

Protection is probabilistic; ADH1B-associated protection should not be equated with a universal systemic flush reaction.

evidence.reference_title: The genetics of alcohol metabolism: role of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase variants.
evidence.snippet: Acetaldehyde is a toxic substance whose accumulation leads to a highly aversive reaction that includes facial flushing, nausea, and rapid heart beat (i.e., tachycardia).

nodes.description: Rodent chronic-intermittent-ethanol studies and cell/slice assays describe time- and compartment-dependent changes in GABA-A receptor surface composition. Reduced tonic ethanol sensitivity can coexist with increased sensitivity of some synaptic currents. Single-dose changes can reverse, while repeated regimens produce longer persistence; endpoint-specific tolerance is not universal receptor loss or proven lifelong human dysfunction. Hippocampal and cortical pyramidal-neuron recordings are among the preparations supporting these changes.

Conditioned taste aversion was attenuated at a moderate 2 g/kg ethanol dose but not at 4 g/kg; details varied by replicate and analysis. Conditioned place preference at the tested 2 g/kg dose did not differ. This genetic co-occurrence does not prove reduced aversion mediates every animal’s intake or absence of all reward differences.

nodes.description: Impaired control and persistent use despite harm are clinical manifestations to which reinforcement, learned cue responses, aversive-state relief and executive-control problems may contribute. These routes can coexist but are not a mandatory ordered sequence, and DSM criteria allow heterogeneous presentations.

nodes.description: Reduced inhibitory control and altered decision-making can contribute to difficulty limiting alcohol use in the addiction framework. Cross-sectional MRI differences in AUD provide anatomical associations, not proof that alcohol caused progressive atrophy or that a measured structural difference mediated an executive deficit.

evidence.reference_title: Neurobiology of addiction: a neurocircuitry analysis.
evidence.snippet: The craving and deficits in executive function in the so-called preoccupation/anticipation stage involve the dysregulation of key afferent projections from the prefrontal cortex and insula, including glutamate, to the basal ganglia and extended amygdala.

evidence.reference_title: How do substance use disorders compare to other psychiatric conditions on structural brain abnormalities? A cross-disorder meta-analytic comparison using the ENIGMA consortium findings.
evidence.snippet: On measures of cortical thickness, AUD was associated with significant differences bilaterally in the fusiform gyrus, inferior temporal gyrus, temporal pole, superior frontal gyrus, and rostral and caudal anterior cingulate gyri.

nodes.description: Difficulties with inhibitory control and decision-making are described in addiction models and some patients with AUD. Their extent, timing and contribution to drinking vary; cross-sectional brain anatomy alone does not establish cognitive dysfunction or its causal direction.

nodes.description: First-line opioid-receptor antagonist for adults with moderate to severe AUD seeking abstinence or reduced drinking. Oral 50 mg/day has the strongest formulation-specific trial evidence for reducing return to heavy drinking; pair with appropriate psychosocial support and patient-defined goals. Current opioid use and acute hepatitis or liver failure are important contraindications; assess future opioid analgesia needs.

nodes.description: Common-variant associations contribute to liability rather than determining disease. The 2023 meta-analysis combines 165,952 AUD or dependence cases, controls and AUDIT problems scores in 1,079,947 participants; it is not a cohort of one million diagnosed cases. The 110 variants are the union of within- and cross-ancestry results, and most data are European ancestry. Specific nonmetabolic variant-to-neural causal routes remain unresolved.

nodes.description: Give thiamine promptly to prevent or treat deficiency-related neurologic injury. Glucose can be given before, after or concurrently; urgent glucose should not be delayed while awaiting thiamine.

nodes.description: Anxiety, dysphoria and other aversive states can motivate renewed drinking for relief. Hyperkatifeia is a cross-drug heuristic framework integrating reward deficits and stress signaling, not a biomarker or a required stage in every patient. Persistent symptoms also require assessment for independent psychiatric illness.

evidence.reference_title: Drug Addiction: Hyperkatifeia/Negative Reinforcement as a Framework for Medications Development.
evidence.snippet: This review focuses on neurochemical/neurocircuitry dysregulations that contribute to hyperkatifeia, defined as a greater intensity of negative emotional/motivational signs and symptoms during withdrawal from drugs of abuse in the withdrawal/negative affect stage of the addiction cycle.

nodes.description: Reviewed dependence models show reduced dopamine neuronal activity or basal striatal dopamine during withdrawal. These observations support a reward-deficit hypothesis but should not be generalized to every brain region, exposure phase or individual with AUD.

evidence.reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
evidence.snippet: By contrast, withdrawal from chronic alcohol exposure has been reported to result in decreased VTA dopamine neuronal activity (Diana et al., 1996; Bailey et al., 2001), and reduced basal levels of dopamine in ventral and dorsal subregions of the striatum, possibly due to enhanced dopamine uptake (Weiss et al., 1996; Budygin et al., 2007; Barak et al., 2011).
